title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
description: Brute force to optimized: walking the range on every call versus a precomputed prefix sum array.

blocks.text: Design a data structure that, given a fixed integer array nums, can efficiently answer multiple queries asking for the sum of elements between two indices left and right (inclusive).

blocks.caption: Precompute prefix sums once, then answer every range query with a single subtraction

blocks.text: Design a data structure that, given a fixed integer array nums, can efficiently answer multiple queries asking for the sum of elements between two indices left and right (inclusive).

blocks.title: Analogy: A Running Odometer Reading for Instant Trip Distances
blocks.text: Like a car's odometer that records the total distance traveled at every single mile marker; to find the distance between any two markers, there is no need to re-drive the route, just subtract one odometer reading from another.

blocks.caption: The distance between two points is just the difference between two running readings

blocks.content: {"headers":["Query","Result","Why"],"rows":[["sumRange(0, 2)","-2 + 0 + 3 = 1","This sums exactly the three elements from index 0 through index 2, inclusive of both endpoints"],["sumRange(2, 5)","3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -1","This sums the four elements from index 2 through index 5, a completely different, overlapping range than the previous query"],["sumRange(0, 5)","-2 + 0 + 3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -3","This sums the entire array, since the range spans from the very first index to the very last"]]}

blocks.text: When left and right refer to the same index, sumRange should return just that single element's value, since the range contains exactly one element, giving for example sumRange(3, 3) equal to nums[3] alone, which here is -5.

Before writing any code, notice the defining feature of this problem: the same array is queried over and over, many times, and it never changes in between. That single fact is what should shape the entire approach, since anything computed once can be reused across every future query.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A single sumRange call can always be answered correctly by just walking from left to right and adding up every element in between, but doing that fresh for every one of potentially thousands of queries repeats an enormous amount of identical work, since many queries overlap heavily with each other.

Observation 2: What actually changes between two different range-sum answers is only which elements are included, and that is completely determined by two boundaries, so if the running total up to any given index were already known in advance, any range sum could be recovered by simple subtraction instead of a fresh walk.

Observation 3: Precomputing, once, the cumulative sum of every prefix of the array, the sum of the first 0 elements, the first 1 element, the first 2 elements, and so on, captures exactly that running total at every possible boundary, all in a single O(n) pass done just once, at construction time.

Observation 4: Once that prefix array exists, the sum of any range from left to right is just prefix[right + 1] minus prefix[left], since the larger prefix already includes everything the smaller one does, plus exactly the extra elements the range actually needs, and subtracting removes exactly the part that should not be counted.

Whenever the same fixed data is queried repeatedly for a range sum, precompute a running prefix sum once, and answer every future range query with a single subtraction instead of ever re-scanning the data.

This prefix sum idea is one of the most foundational and widely reused techniques in all of array processing, appearing again and again whenever a problem needs fast, repeated access to the sum, count, or aggregate of a contiguous range.
Store the array directly, and for every sumRange call, walk from left to right, adding up every element along the way.

items: Store the input array as-is in the constructor, with no precomputation at all.
For every sumRange(left, right) call, loop from index left to index right, adding each element to a running total.
Return that running total once the loop finishes.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The constructor does nothing beyond storing a reference to the array, since the brute force intentionally defers all actual work to query time rather than doing any upfront preparation.
The loop bound is left to right inclusive, not exclusive, since the range sumRange(left, right) is explicitly defined to include both endpoints.
A running total is accumulated with a simple addition inside the loop, rather than any more complex bookkeeping, since a plain sum is all a single, isolated query needs.

blocks.text: Every element within the requested range is directly added exactly once, so the returned sum is always correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for the constructor, but O(n) for every single sumRange call in the worst case, since a call spanning the whole array walks every element.
Space: O(n), for storing a copy of, or reference to, the original array.

Limitation: if sumRange is called q times, the total work across all queries can reach O(n times q) in the worst case, which becomes very slow once both the array and the number of queries grow large, even though the array itself never changes between calls.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's real waste is temporal, not logical: it re-derives, from scratch, the exact same running totals for overlapping portions of the array on every single call, even though nums never changes between one query and the next. If that running total were computed once, ahead of time, for every possible starting boundary, the specific value needed for any future range query would already be sitting there, ready to be looked up instead of recomputed. Concretely, keeping a running cumulative sum, prefix[i] equal to the sum of the first i elements, lets any range sum from left to right be recovered as prefix[right + 1] minus prefix[left], since prefix[right + 1] already includes the range being asked about, and everything before it, and subtracting prefix[left] removes exactly that extra leading part, leaving only the range itself. This shifts all the real work into a single O(n) pass done once, at construction time, leaving each individual query as a single O(1) subtraction.

Precompute a prefix sum array in the constructor, where prefix[i] holds the sum of the first i elements of nums, with prefix[0] equal to 0, representing an empty prefix. Then sumRange(left, right) is answered directly as prefix[right + 1] minus prefix[left], a single subtraction with no loop needed at query time at all.
Build the prefix sum array once, then answer every query with a single subtraction.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Build prefix array: prefix[0] = 0","starts at 0, representing the sum of zero elements","An empty prefix has nothing in it, so its sum is trivially 0, which is what makes the subtraction formula work correctly even for a range starting at index 0"],["prefix[1] = prefix[0] + nums[0] = 0 + (-2) = -2","running total after including nums[0]","Each prefix entry adds exactly one more element to the running total from the previous entry"],["Continuing: prefix = [0, -2, -2, 1, -4, -2, -3]","the complete prefix array, one entry longer than nums","Every one of the 6 elements of nums has now been folded into a running cumulative total, with one extra leading 0"],["sumRange(0, 2): prefix[3] - prefix[0] = 1 - 0 = 1","matches the direct sum of -2 + 0 + 3","prefix[3] already includes everything from index 0 through index 2, and prefix[0] is 0, so the subtraction leaves exactly that range's sum"],["sumRange(2, 5): prefix[6] - prefix[2] = -3 - (-2) = -1","matches the direct sum of 3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1)","prefix[6] includes everything through index 5, and prefix[2] includes everything up through index 1; subtracting removes exactly the part before index 2, leaving indices 2 through 5"]]}

blocks.caption: Building the prefix array once, then reading off any range sum as a single subtraction

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) for the constructor's one-time prefix computation, and O(1) for every individual sumRange call afterward.
Space: O(n), for the prefix array, one element longer than the original array.

prefix[i] is defined as the sum of nums[0] through nums[i-1], so prefix[right+1] is the sum of everything from the start of the array up through index right, and prefix[left] is the sum of everything from the start up through index left minus 1, exactly the part that should not be included in the range. Subtracting the second from the first cancels out that unwanted leading portion entirely, leaving precisely the sum of nums[left] through nums[right], with no element double-counted or missed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Expression","What it represents"],"rows":[["prefix[right + 1]","The sum of every element from index 0 up to and including index right"],["prefix[left]","The sum of every element from index 0 up to but not including index left, exactly the portion to exclude"],["prefix[right + 1] minus prefix[left]","The sum of exactly the elements from index left to index right, inclusive"]]}

items: The prefix array is allocated with one extra slot beyond nums' own length, since prefix[0] represents the sum of zero elements, a value that has no corresponding index in nums itself.
Each entry is built directly from the previous one, so the entire array is constructed in a single linear pass, never revisiting an earlier element.

sumRange itself contains no loop at all, just one array lookup for each of the two prefix values and one subtraction, which is what makes every single query O(1) regardless of how wide the requested range is.
The off-by-one shift, using prefix[right + 1] rather than prefix[right], is what correctly makes the upper bound of the query inclusive, matching the problem's own definition of sumRange.

blocks.text: This problem is the foundational, textbook introduction to the prefix sum technique: whenever the same fixed array needs repeated range-sum queries, trading a one-time O(n) preprocessing cost for O(1) per query is almost always the right move.

items: Off-by-one errors in the prefix array's indexing, most commonly forgetting the extra leading 0 slot, which shifts every subsequent lookup by one position and silently produces wrong answers.
Recomputing the prefix sums, or any part of them, inside sumRange itself, instead of doing it once in the constructor, which defeats the entire purpose of the optimization.
Using prefix[right] instead of prefix[right + 1], which would incorrectly exclude the element at index right from the range sum, since sumRange's right boundary is meant to be inclusive.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A query where left equals right","Correctly returns just that single element's value, since prefix[right + 1] minus prefix[left] collapses to exactly one element's contribution"],["A query covering the entire array","Correctly returns the total sum of the whole array, since the final prefix entry holds the complete running total and prefix[0] is 0"]]}

items: Explicitly name the technique as "prefix sums" and mention its O(n) construction plus O(1) query tradeoff up front, since interviewers are often specifically listening for that vocabulary and complexity framing on this exact problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "The same array or data is queried repeatedly for a range sum, or range aggregate, and the data itself does not change" points toward prefix sums: precompute cumulative totals once, then answer every future range query with a single subtraction.

items: What if the array could be updated between queries, a mix of point updates and range sum queries? A plain prefix sum array breaks down, since a single update would require rebuilding the entire array; a Fenwick tree, also called a Binary Indexed Tree, or a segment tree supports both operations in O(log n) each instead.

How would you extend this to a 2D grid, answering sum queries over rectangular sub-regions? Build a 2D prefix sum table using inclusion-exclusion, adding and subtracting overlapping rectangular regions, generalizing the same one-subtraction-per-query idea to two dimensions.

What if queries needed the product of a range instead of the sum? The same prefix technique applies directly using running products instead of running sums, as long as division by zero, from a zero element in the array, is handled carefully, since it breaks the simple prefix-division approach.
The direct foundation for every other prefix-sum problem in this category, including Subarray Sum Equals K, Product of Array Except Self, and Range Sum Query 2D.
Same "precompute once, query in O(1) forever after" philosophy as building a lookup table or memoization cache for any repeatedly-queried, unchanging piece of data.
Same underlying cumulative-total idea used in Kadane's Algorithm and various sliding window problems, where a running sum is maintained incrementally rather than recomputed.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) construction, O(n) per query, O(n) space.
Optimized (prefix sums): O(n) construction, O(1) per query, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Prefix sum precomputation for O(1) repeated range-sum queries
Core Idea: Precompute a running cumulative sum once at construction time, then answer any range sum as a single subtraction between two prefix values
Time: O(n) to build, O(1) per query
Space: O(n), for the prefix array
Most Important Observation: When the same fixed array is queried repeatedly for range sums, moving all the real work into a one-time O(n) setup makes every future query O(1)
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: prefix[right plus 1] minus prefix[left] is the whole trick
